segments.text: Sociology begins with a simple idea: human beings develop and live through relationships with other people. “Sociality of man” means that human behaviour, identity and daily life are deeply shaped by interaction, culture, groups and institutions.
This is a short syllabus point, but it is conceptually important because it explains why sociology does not study the individual in isolation.

items.text: Meaning of sociality
: Sociality refers to the human capacity and tendency to form relationships, groups, roles and shared ways of life. Humans depend on others for care, language, learning, cooperation and identity.
Individual and society

: Individuals have agency and personal differences, but they are born into pre-existing languages, norms and institutions. Society influences action, while people also reproduce and change society through their actions.
Socialization
: Through socialization, people learn language, values, norms, roles and expectations. Family, peers, schools, media, workplaces and other institutions all contribute.
Sociological imagination

: A sociological way of thinking connects personal experience with wider social structure and history. For example, unemployment may be experienced individually but can also reflect labour-market conditions.

blocks.text: Why human beings are social without denying individuality

segments.text: Sociology begins from a simple observation: people become recognizably human persons through relationships, language, institutions and culture. Biological capacities matter, but a child does not acquire language, moral rules, role expectations or a sense of social identity in isolation. At the same time, society is not an external machine acting on passive individuals; institutions are reproduced and changed through human action.

items.text: Sociality
: Sociality refers to the human capacity and tendency to form relationships, groups and patterned interaction. Cooperation, conflict, care, exchange and communication are all forms of social life.
Individual agency
: Agency is the capacity to make choices and act, although choices are made within opportunities and constraints created by class, gender, family, law, culture and other structures.
Social structure

: Social structure refers to relatively enduring patterns of roles, relationships and institutions. It shapes what actions are likely or possible without mechanically determining every individual decision.
Biological foundation

: Humans are born with biological needs and capacities, including capacities for learning and attachment. Biological development sets possibilities and constraints, but does not provide a finished culture or identity.
Social environment
: Caregivers, peers, schools, media and institutions provide language, norms and models. Through interaction, children learn what behaviours are expected and how others respond to them.
Interaction rather than opposition

: The useful question is not whether nature or nurture is more important in general. Development emerges from interaction: biological capacities make learning possible, while social environments shape which capacities are practised and rewarded.

blocks.text: Socialization: how society becomes part of the person

items.text: Primary socialization

: Early family and caregiving relationships teach language, basic trust, self-control, manners and fundamental categories of social life. It is powerful because the child has few alternative reference groups.
Secondary socialization
: Later institutions such as school, workplace, military, professional organizations and peer groups teach specialized roles and expectations.
Anticipatory socialization
: People may rehearse values and behaviours associated with a group they expect or hope to join, such as a profession.
Resocialization

: Major transitions can require old routines to be replaced by new ones. Total institutions are an extreme case, but ordinary migration, marriage or occupational change can also require resocialization.
Socialization is not perfect conformity

: People interpret, negotiate and sometimes resist norms. Socialization creates shared expectations but also produces variation because people occupy different positions and encounter different experiences.
Cooley's looking-glass self

: Cooley argued that the self develops partly through imagining how we appear to others, imagining their judgment and developing feelings about ourselves. The point is not that people accurately know others' judgments, but that perceived social evaluation helps shape identity.
Mead's I and Me

: George Herbert Mead distinguished the spontaneous 'I' from the socialized 'Me', the organized expectations of others that a person can take into account. The self develops through role-taking and symbolic interaction.
Generalized other
: As children mature, they learn not only the expectations of specific people but broader rules of the group or community. This generalized perspective enables participation in organized social life.
Identity
: Identity combines self-understanding with social categories and roles. People hold multiple identities, and their importance changes with setting and life stage.
Family

: Provides early language, emotional relationships, class position, religious or cultural practices and basic norms. Families vary greatly, so sociology studies patterns without assuming one universal form.
School
: Schools transmit formal knowledge and also a hidden curriculum of punctuality, competition, cooperation, authority and evaluation.
Peer groups
: Peers become especially influential in adolescence and youth because they provide belonging, comparison and norms outside the family.
Media and digital platforms
: Media circulate models of lifestyle, gender, success, consumption and politics. Audiences do not absorb messages passively, but repeated exposure can shape agendas and available cultural scripts.
Workplace
: Occupations teach technical roles, professional ethics, hierarchy and organizational culture. Work socialization continues throughout adult life.

blocks.text: Social isolation as evidence for sociality

segments.text: Historical cases of severe childhood isolation are frequently discussed because they illustrate how language and social development depend on interaction. Such cases must be interpreted cautiously: they often involve neglect, trauma and incomplete records, so they cannot function as controlled experiments. Their value is to show that human development requires sustained social relationships, not to establish a simple nature-versus-nurture percentage.

rows: Avoid this error Do not write that society completely controls the individual. Sociology studies both social constraints and human agency.

blocks.text: How to Build an Examination Answer

segments.text: Define sociality, explain dependence on social interaction and socialization, show the two-way relationship between individual and society, and use one everyday example.
• Conerly, Holmes, & Tamang, Introduction to Sociology 3e (OpenStax, 2021).
• Cooley, Human Nature and the Social Order; George Herbert Mead, Mind, Self, and Society.
• Humans are social beings because much human development depends on interaction.
• Society shapes individuals, but individuals also influence society.
• Socialization transmits culture and prepares people for social roles.
• Sociology links personal experience with wider social patterns.
• Connect definitions with mechanisms, examples and limitations; do not present the topic as a list of isolated terms.
